title: How much food to store, and what
summary: Agencies say to store from several days to 30 days of food; the Red Cross says 2 weeks at home, and this app plans for at least 2 weeks, the same as for water. Build up from the food your household already eats: food that needs no refrigeration, little or no cooking and little or no water. Plan for babies, children, older people, special diets and pets. No source opened gives an amount of food per person for an emergency, or any amount for a child.

blocks.p: Agencies give different numbers of days:

list: Ready.gov (FEMA): at least a several-day supply of non-perishable food.
New York State’s preparedness checklist: at least enough food for 7 days. New York State Division of Homeland Security and Emergency Services: be prepared to make it on your own for at least 10 days.
American Red Cross: a 2-week supply for home, and a 3-day supply to take with you if you leave.
FEMA, the Red Cross and USDA, in an older booklet: even though it is unlikely that an emergency would cut off your food supply for two weeks, prepare a supply that will last that long.
University of Illinois Extension: enough food for each person in the household for 14 to 30 days.
Oregon State University Extension: Oregon’s minimum goal is meals for 2 weeks, and many local emergency managers there recommend 4 weeks.

blocks.p: This app plans for at least 2 weeks of food at home, the Red Cross figure, the same as How much water you need does for water. The longest figure in any source opened is 30 days (University of Illinois Extension).

sections.h: Build it up from what you eat now

steps: List everyone in the household by name, with any special needs such as diabetes or allergies (University of Georgia Extension, University of Minnesota Extension).

Write down the meals for each day, for 14 days (University of Minnesota Extension). On each day’s list, note how much water and what equipment and utensils the meals need (University of Georgia Extension).
Check your cupboards. Many people already have a two-week supply of most staples once they make a written plan (University of Georgia Extension).
Buy more of the basic foods you normally keep on your shelves. That is the easiest way to build a two-week supply (FEMA, Red Cross and USDA booklet).
If you eat out regularly, add those meals to your list (University of Georgia Extension, University of Illinois Extension).
Date what you buy and keep it so it lasts, as in Store food so it lasts.

blocks.p: You don’t need to buy unfamiliar foods. Familiar foods are important: they can lift morale and give a feeling of security in time of stress (FEMA, Red Cross and USDA booklet).

Choose foods your family will eat (Ready.gov). Foods that need no refrigeration, preparation or cooking are best (FEMA, Red Cross and USDA booklet), and foods that need little or no water (University of Georgia Extension).

list: Ready-to-eat canned meats, fish, poultry, beans, fruits, vegetables, pasta, soup and juice (Ready.gov, New York State Division of Homeland Security and Emergency Services).
Protein or fruit bars, dry cereal or granola (Ready.gov).
High-energy foods: peanut butter, jelly, nuts, dried meat such as jerky, granola, trail mix, energy bars (New York State Division of Homeland Security and Emergency Services).
Dried fruit and canned juices (Ready.gov).
Milk that keeps on the shelf: powdered, canned or shelf-stable brick pack (New York State Division of Homeland Security and Emergency Services).
Staples: sugar, salt, pepper, instant coffee, tea bags, cocoa (New York State Division of Homeland Security and Emergency Services).
Comfort foods, such as chocolate bars and hard candy (Ready.gov, New York State Division of Homeland Security and Emergency Services).
Food for babies, older people and anyone on a special diet (Ready.gov, New York State Division of Homeland Security and Emergency Services).
Food for pets (Ready.gov, University of Illinois Extension).

If some of your food needs cooking, keep some that is ready to eat too (University of Georgia Extension). Canned food is already cooked and can be eaten right out of the can (University of Georgia Extension; FEMA, Red Cross and USDA booklet).

Don’t buy large or institutional-size containers to save money if you won’t be able to store the leftovers properly (University of Georgia Extension). How long opened food may sit out is in Is it still good?
Keep a manual can opener (Ready.gov).
Work out how much extra fuel you need to cook for 2 to 4 weeks (Oregon State University Extension). Where and how to cook safely is in Cook without power.
Plan water for food that needs it, such as instant oatmeal, dry milk, powdered drink mixes, dried soups, bouillon, and instant rice and potatoes (University of Georgia Extension).

Dehydrated and freeze-dried foods are light and take little room, but need extra water to make them ready to eat (University of Georgia Extension). You also need more water to digest freeze-dried food (Oregon State University Extension).
Don’t stock salty foods if your water may be limited: they make you thirsty (FEMA, Red Cross and USDA booklet).

blocks.p: How much water to store, and how to store it, is in the water topics.

list: Babies, toddlers and older people, and anyone with a special diet or allergies, need particular attention (FEMA, Red Cross and USDA booklet).
If you have a baby, stock infant formula, bottles and baby food (Ready.gov Build A Kit, American Red Cross). Never buy or use formula after its Use-By date (USDA).
Stock foods your children already eat: a disaster is not the time to surprise young children with new foods (Oregon State University Extension).
Food for special diets, allergies or medical needs (University of Illinois Extension). Canned dietetic foods, juices and soups may help people who are ill or older (FEMA, Red Cross and USDA booklet).

blocks.p: No source opened gives an amount of food for a child, so this app gives none.

No current federal, New York State or extension source opened gives an amount of food per person per day for an emergency store. Oregon State University Extension builds its emergency pantry list on MyPlate’s plan for 2,000 calories a day, for ages 14 and up, and says the number of servings and portion sizes vary with age and activity level. After a disaster, people may be far more active outdoors than usual (Oregon State University Extension).
This app works out no calorie or weight figure of its own.

sections.h: Storing for a year: one extension list

blocks.p: University of Georgia Extension (page reviewed 2017) suggests these amounts “per adult, per year” of bulk staples, best bought in nitrogen-packed cans. The page names an older FEMA booklet (2004) and a church preparedness manual (1998) as its references without saying which gave the figures. It gives nothing for children, and for babies says “Amounts needed would vary, depending on the age of the infant.” This app does not turn these figures into amounts for fewer days, for a household or for a child.

Per adult, per year
